sources.title: Bauhaus-Archiv — “14 Years of Bauhaus” chronology
sources.supports: Best concise first-party chronology of locations, directors, workshops, exhibitions, political pressure, closure, and emigration.

sources.title: Bauhaus-Archiv — *About Bauhaus*
sources.supports: Institution’s podcast project explicitly revisits legends and clichés; useful as an editorial anti-cliché spine.

sources.title: Bauhaus-Archiv — “How the memory of the Bauhaus was rescued”
sources.supports: Reception history, Nazi conditions imposed on the Berlin school, migration, and the powerful role of the 1938 MoMA narrative.

sources.title: Bauhaus Dessau Foundation — chronology
sources.supports: Strong source for the productive Dessau years, Hannes Meyer’s social/scientific approach, political conflict, and later historiography.

sources.title: Bauhaus Dessau Foundation — Collection Department
sources.supports: Archive/library/image holdings; establishes the scale and Dessau focus of the second-largest historic Bauhaus collection.

sources.title: Bauhaus Dessau Foundation — Curatorial Workshop
sources.supports: Connects historic workshop pedagogy to experimentation, learning, display politics, and current research—not a frozen “look.”

sources.title: Bauhaus Dessau Foundation — Education
sources.supports: Clear public-history explanation of how students learned through workshops and how the buildings/collection are interpreted today.

sources.title: Klassik Stiftung Weimar — Haus Am Horn
sources.supports: Authoritative source on the 1923 model house as a cross-workshop prototype for modern living, materials, technology, and furnishing.

sources.title: Klassik Stiftung Weimar — Bauhaus collections
sources.supports: Primary collection overview focused on 1919–25 Weimar: studies, typography, craft, design objects, photographs, and documents.

sources.title: UNESCO — Bauhaus and its Sites in Weimar, Dessau and Bernau
sources.supports: Authoritative architectural heritage scope and significance; prevents reducing “Bauhaus architecture” to one façade.

sources.title: MoMA — *Bauhaus 1919–1933: Workshops for Modernity*
sources.supports: Major museum synthesis organized around workshops and lived historical change, not a single visual formula.

sources.title: MoMA — exhibition checklist PDF
sources.supports: Object-level map across painting, craft, stage, typography, photography, furniture, architecture, and student work.

sources.title: The Met — “The Bauhaus, 1919–1933”
sources.supports: Reliable overview of phases, directors, political/financial instability, curriculum, and objects.

sources.title: Getty Research Institute — *Bauhaus Beginnings*
sources.supports: Corrective to the machine-age cliché: early spiritual, expressionist, pedagogical, and material exercises.

sources.title: Getty — *Bauhaus: Building the New Artist* launch
sources.supports: Source for the digital archive/exercise project and the school’s learn-by-doing methods.

sources.title: Harvard Art Museums — *The Bauhaus and Harvard* introduction
sources.supports: Museum account of pedagogy, workshops, everyday life, migration, and American institutional transmission.

sources.title: Harvard Art Museums — *Object Lessons: The Bauhaus and Harvard*
sources.supports: Scholarship explicitly expands weaving, photography, work by women, and the 30,000-object Harvard Bauhaus resource.

sources.title: Josef & Anni Albers Foundation — biography
sources.supports: Foundation chronology of both artists, Anni’s Jewish identity, workshop constraints, teaching, exile, and Black Mountain/Yale transmission.

sources.title: Josef & Anni Albers Foundation — teaching
sources.supports: Specific source on preliminary-course experimentation and Anni Albers’s weaving pedagogy, acting directorship, and material research.

sources.title: Architectural Digest (2023) — “Bauhaus Interior Design”
sources.supports: Mainstream current definition to audit: useful for what consumers expect, but should be balanced by the workshop and critical tiers.

sources.title: Wallpaper* (2026) — Jil Sander × Thonet
sources.supports: Contemporary licensed-manufacturer reinterpretation of Breuer, Stam, Mies, and tubular-steel development.

sources.title: Wallpaper* (2026) — Anni Albers guide
sources.supports: Recent textile-centered account of material experiment, gendered workshop routing, exile, jewelry, teaching, and modernist networks.

sources.title: Livingetc (2026) — “What Are ‘Bauhaus Colors’?”
sources.supports: Direct evidence of how the primary-color shorthand is marketed in interiors; use as present-day reception, not as sole history.

sources.title: Wallpaper* (2025) — Gropius House public-toilet competition
sources.supports: Living heritage/practice example where accessibility, visitor needs, innovation, and site character matter more than imitation.

sources.title: Wallpaper* (2026) — Triennale uniforms and Bauhaus-inspired geometries
sources.supports: Current cross-disciplinary use in workwear, folding, hospitality, and institutional identity.

sources.title: Frieze — “Women of the Bauhaus”
sources.supports: Clear account of gendered workshop steering and the gap between women’s contribution and canonical recognition.

sources.title: European Parliament Research Service — *The Bauhaus movement: Where are the women?*
sources.supports: Reputable institutional briefing on access, curriculum, gender hierarchy, and historical visibility.

sources.title: Klassik Stiftung Weimar — *Bauhaus and National Socialism*
sources.supports: Essential correction to a simple “Bauhaus good / Nazis closed it” story: political conflicts, later accommodation, persecution, and individual choices.

sources.title: bauhaus imaginista
sources.supports: Transcultural project on global conversations, vernacular practice, non-European modernisms, and the limits of a unified Western export story.

sources.title: Bauhaus Dessau Foundation — Study Rooms 2026
sources.supports: Current institutional self-critique: industrial extraction, environmental degradation, labor/care, layered histories, and contradictions in Bauhaus legacies.
